essentials: OFAC's rule that an entity 50% or more owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more blocked persons is itself considered blocked — even if its own name is not on any sanctions list.

The Federal Reserve's current operating framework, in which reserves are supplied to the banking system on demand at the policy rate, rather than tightly rationed — since 2020 the US reserve requirement ratio has been zero.
The IMF's examination of each member's economy, usually annual, under Article IV of its Articles of Agreement, publishing a staff report and the Executive Board's assessment.
The double-entry accounting record of a country's transactions with the rest of the world, which always balances by construction — current and capital account balances mirror the financial account.
When depositors withdraw from a bank because they expect other depositors to withdraw, which can fail an otherwise solvent bank purely on that self-fulfilling expectation.

term: BIS central bank policy rates database
essentials: The Bank for International Settlements' own compiled dataset of policy rates across central banks worldwide, updated daily.
A currency issued by software rather than a state, created by a 2008 whitepaper describing a peer-to-peer electronic cash system with a fixed, algorithmically-set supply.
The standard academic entry point for Bitcoin's economics, technology and governance, surveying the design for a general economics audience.
16 September 1992, when the UK suspended sterling's membership of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism after "heavy official purchases of sterling" failed to hold the currency inside its band.
The 1944 agreement that pegged currencies to the US dollar, and the dollar to gold, until 1971.
The National Bureau of Economic Research body whose announcements are the official record of when a US recession began and ended.
A central bank's own published record of its assets (bond holdings, lending) and liabilities (currency in circulation, bank reserves), typically disclosed weekly.
An early BIS term for what is now generally called a central bank digital currency, from the BIS's 2017 analysis comparing crypto-style issuance and settlement to central-bank money.
A digital claim directly on a central bank — unlike ordinary digital money in a bank account, which is a claim on a commercial bank and carries that bank's credit risk.
The principle that a central bank sets interest rates without day-to-day direction from elected government, to keep monetary policy free of short-term political pressure.

Cross-country indices scoring how legally independent a central bank is from its government; studies using them found more independent central banks associated with lower, less variable inflation and no cost to growth.
The result that delegating monetary policy to a central banker who weights inflation more heavily than society as a whole does can reduce the inflation bias that comes from time inconsistency.
The standard measure of inflation, tracking the price of a fixed basket of goods and services over time; "core" inflation excludes volatile food and energy prices.
How a payment actually crosses a border — a chain of banks holding accounts with each other, with the payment message travelling separately from the money itself.

An exchange-rate regime in which a currency is fully backed by, and fixed to, a foreign reserve currency, with no independent monetary policy — Hong Kong's linked exchange rate system is a documented example.
An event in which a speculative attack forces a fixed or managed exchange rate to break; economists group the explanations into three model "generations" built for different real episodes.

A reclassification of countries' exchange-rate regimes based on what currencies actually did, rather than what governments officially announced — often finding a country's real regime differed from its stated one.

The documented decline in active correspondent-banking relationships — about a fifth between 2011 and 2018 even as payment volumes rose — concentrated in small, poor and higher-risk jurisdictions, driven by compliance cost and risk aversion.

How much of a policy-rate change a bank actually passes through to what it pays savers; ECB research found roughly 68% reaches new household term deposits but only 23% reaches ordinary overnight deposits.
A guarantee, up to a set limit, that a depositor's money is protected if their bank fails — removing the incentive to be first in line during a run.

An unsettled empirical debate — one study finds program participation associated with lower growth in the years after, another finds effects depend on how well a country complies with its conditions — complicated by the fact that countries in trouble are the ones that borrow.
Research documenting how much of global trade is invoiced in a small number of "vehicle" currencies, dominated by the US dollar, independent of which countries are actually trading with each other.
New Zealand adopted the first formal inflation target in 1990, followed by Canada in 1991 and the United Kingdom in 1992; by the late 1990s the framework was standard among advanced economies.
The European Union framework under which member states adopt the euro and cede national monetary policy to the European Central Bank.
The result that a proof-of-work system's security rests on the cost of attacking it, which in turn implies a mathematical limit on the value such a system can safely secure.
The European Central Bank's own daily published exchange rates between the euro and other major currencies.
The system that pegged European currencies to each other within set bands before the euro, and from which the UK and Italy were forced out in September 1992.

How much of a currency's move actually reaches domestic prices; a BIS study of several industrialised economies found the overall effect "modest," but stronger in countries with a larger import share.
The rule a country chooses for how its currency's price is set, from a free float to giving up its own currency entirely.
The Federal Reserve committee that meets eight times a year to set the US policy rate.
Legal measures — asset freezes and trade restrictions — that a government uses to block transactions with a named person, entity or jurisdiction.

The framework the Federal Reserve adopted in 2020, aiming for inflation moderately above its 2% target for some time after periods running below it, to average out over time rather than target every period identically.
A central bank telling the public what it expects to do with its policy rate in the future, which can move longer-term borrowing costs before any decision is actually made.

The set of technical work areas the Financial Stability Board organised its cross-border payments improvement programme around, each targeting a specific documented friction — cost, speed, access or transparency.

Numerical targets the Financial Stability Board set for 2027 — a global average cost of no more than 1% for retail payments (3% for remittances), 75% of payments credited within one hour, plus access and transparency goals.

term: General principles for international remittance services
essentials: Joint CPMI–World Bank principles describing the chain a remittance passes through — sending agent, settlement between institutions, paying agent — and what cost and transparency disclosure should look like.

The Federal Reserve does not own gold itself; the US Treasury does, and the Fed holds gold certificates against it — one reason gold's price can still move on shifts in currency confidence even though no currency is convertible into it.
The United States suspended domestic gold convertibility for citizens in 1933 and revalued gold from $20.67 to $35 an ounce in 1934, a real, dated step in the gold standard's interwar unwinding.
Gold central banks hold as a reserve asset today, valued daily against the LBMA Gold Price and reported to the IMF, with no currency convertible into it anymore.
The system, roughly 1870 to 1914, in which a currency was defined as a fixed weight of gold and could be exchanged for it on demand.

The weaker, revived form of the gold standard in the 1920s, in which central banks held other countries' currencies as reserves alongside gold; when the Depression came, the commitment to gold forced monetary contraction, and countries that left gold early recovered sooner.
The thesis that the gold standard's rigid rules worsened and spread the Great Depression, forcing countries to tighten monetary policy exactly when their economies needed the opposite.

The Federal Reserve's own name for the 1965–1982 US inflation episode, ended only after the FOMC's October 1979 shift to explicitly targeting money-stock growth — a sustained policy-framework change, not something that resolved on its own.
A way of moving money across borders on trust between dealers, with no money actually crossing.
A run of a central bank's decisions in one direction — a sequence of rate increases (a hiking cycle) or decreases (an easing cycle) — before it changes course.
Long-run historical research on how the composition of the world's reserve currencies has shifted over time, and what has historically driven a currency's rise or fall in international use.
Policy changes a country agrees to in exchange for IMF lending, released in tranches as the country meets the agreed conditions.
A Board of Governors — one per member, usually the finance minister or central bank governor — sits above an Executive Board that takes day-to-day decisions; voting power follows each member's quota.
The amount a country pays into the IMF, which determines how much it can borrow and how many votes it holds — broadly reflecting the size of its economy.
The proposition that a country cannot simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy — it must give up one of the three.
The framework in which a central bank commits to a numerical inflation goal, usually 2%, and explains its decisions against it.

Two competing models of what a bank does when it lends — one where a bank merely channels existing savings, one where lending itself creates new deposits — with materially different predictions for how bank lending affects the economy.
A club of almost every country in the world, created at Bretton Woods in 1944, that pools members' quota payments and lends to a member that cannot pay for its imports or service its foreign debt.
The Federal Reserve's own term for quantitative easing; it ran three rounds from late 2008 and a fourth from March 2020, taking its balance sheet from under $1 trillion to nearly $9 trillion.
A central bank facility letting a bank borrow against collateral during a liquidity squeeze, rather than being forced to sell assets into a falling market to meet withdrawals.
A phone-based e-money account, moved between phones and converted to and from cash through a network of local agents rather than bank branches.

Official measures of the money supply, defined differently by jurisdiction; US definitions changed materially in 2020 when savings deposits were reclassified into M1, so long time series must be read with that definitional break in mind.
The Federal Reserve's own 2022 discussion paper setting out the possible benefits and risks of a US central bank digital currency, and how it would compare with existing digital money.
The process by which commercial banks create new deposits — new money — the moment they make a loan, rather than simply lending out money customers have already deposited.

Disguising the origin of illegally obtained money so it appears to come from a legitimate source; a documented concern for informal transfer systems that regulators track alongside terrorist-financing risk.

The staggered way higher interest rates reach fixed-rate mortgage holders — only as each household's fixed deal expires and they roll onto a new, higher rate — documented by the Bank of England during the 2022–23 tightening cycle.
The standard modern framework for interest-rate policy, in which a credible inflation objective anchors the public's expectations and shapes how the economy responds to a rate change.
The August 1971 decision that ended the US dollar's convertibility into gold and, within two years, the era of fixed exchange rates.
An account a bank holds at a partner bank abroad, pre-funded so cross-border payments can be settled by adjusting balances rather than moving physical cash.
The European Central Bank's emergency bond-buying programme launched in 2020, alongside its longer-running asset purchase programme, as part of the pandemic monetary-policy response.
The interest rate a central bank sets to steer borrowing costs across an economy.

The main documented channel by which quantitative easing reaches asset prices beyond the bonds actually purchased — investors who sold bonds to the central bank redeploy that money into other assets, pushing up their prices too.

A 2020 review by former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke argues that quantitative easing and forward guidance together provided the equivalent of roughly three percentage points of additional policy-rate cuts, at a time the actual rate was stuck near zero.
A central bank buying large amounts of bonds with newly created reserves to push down longer-term interest rates once its policy rate is already near zero.
A central bank letting its bond holdings shrink — actively or by not reinvesting maturing bonds — reversing quantitative easing.
Wage growth after adjusting for inflation using the Consumer Price Index; real earnings can fall even while nominal pay rises, whenever prices rise faster than the pay increase.
A currency's exchange rate against a broad, trade-weighted basket of its trading partners' currencies, adjusted for inflation differences — a more informative signal than any single bilateral rate.
Money that a migrant worker sends home to family — for many countries, a larger and steadier inflow than foreign investment or foreign aid.
A specific sending-country-to-receiving-country pair for migrant remittances, each with its own set of transfer routes, costs and typical speeds.
The standard academic survey on what drives migrants to remit, how transfers respond to shocks at home, and the evidence on effects on poverty, schooling and investment in receiving countries.

The IMF's own framework for judging whether a country's foreign-currency reserve level is unusual given its trade, debt and capital-flow exposure — the reference most central banks and the IMF itself use.
A currency that other countries' central banks hold, invoice in and borrow in as part of their own official reserves.

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal target to cut the average cost of sending remittances to below 3% by 2030, with no corridor above 5% — against a global average that has hovered around 6%.

Maurice Obstfeld's model treats a currency peg as something a government could defend but might choose not to if the cost outweighs the benefit — meaning an attack can become self-fulfilling once enough speculators believe the government will abandon the peg.
The IMF's own multi-volume history, documenting its transformation from guardian of the Bretton Woods pegs to crisis lender after 1971, with one volume covering the 1980s debt crises specifically.
An IMF-created reserve asset — neither a currency nor a claim on the IMF, but a potential claim on other members' currencies — valued on a basket of five currencies.
A cryptoasset designed to hold a steady value, usually pegged to a currency like the US dollar, through claimed reserves or an algorithm.

aliases: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
essentials: A global cooperative messaging network banks use to send payment instructions to each other; SWIFT itself states it "does not actually move money" — funds move separately, through correspondent banking.
SWIFT's own service for end-to-end tracking of a payment instruction as it moves between the banks in a cross-border chain.

The Swiss National Bank's minimum exchange-rate policy for the franc against the euro, discontinued without warning in January 2015, causing the franc to surge — a documented case of a currency appreciation, not a fall, following a sudden policy exit.
The ECB's 2021 strategy revision replacing its "below, but close to, 2%" formulation with a symmetric 2% target, treating undershoots and overshoots of the target as equally undesirable.
A legal mechanism letting the FDIC protect all deposits at a failed bank — not just the standard $250,000 limit — as it did for Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023.
The Federal Reserve's January 2012 statement was the first time it publicly named an explicit numerical inflation goal of 2%.
An IMF staff note assessing new forms of digital money, including the risks the Fund identified in countries that adopted a cryptocurrency as legal tender.

The problem that a policymaker able to re-optimise every period is tempted to create surprise inflation for a short-term gain; the public anticipates it, and the result is higher inflation with no lasting output benefit.
The chain by which a central bank's rate decision reaches the real economy; central banks themselves describe it as working through "long, variable and uncertain time lags."

A core-inflation measure that removes a price index's most volatile categories, argued to be a less noisy signal of the persistent, policy-relevant component of price growth than the headline figure alone.

A currency used to price trade between two countries even though it is neither country's own currency — a BIS paper notes "international trade is mostly priced in a few key vehicle currencies," which is why a move in that third currency can matter to a trade neither side is directly exposed to.
A plot of a government's bond yields against how long until each bond matures; when a short-dated bond yields more than a long-dated one, the curve is "inverted."

When a short-dated government bond yields more than a long-dated one; the New York Fed's own account states this has preceded every US recession since the 1950s, with a lead time that has varied episode to episode.
